query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, self-lubricating coating of 2D high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoflakes onto a CoCrFeNi matrix will induce an adaptive, tribocatalytic tribofilm that maintains a low friction coefficient and reduced wear rate throughout the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with its standard microstructure and tribological performance characteristics (higher friction and wear at elevated temperatures).
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin layer of 2D HEA nanoflakes (for example, a composition similar to MoWNbTaV–based nanoflakes) onto the CoCrFeNi substrate via a controlled spray coating or vapor deposition process.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under variable load in ambient air, with temperatures ranging continuously from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an adaptive, layered tribofilm at the sliding interface, wherein the 2D nanoflake layer facilitates shear-induced energy dissipation and the catalytic generation of a lubricious phase.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the 2D HEA nanoflake coating’s intrinsically low shear strength and tribocatalytic activity promote the in situ formation of a lubricious tribolayer (e.g., an ultra-nanocrystalline oxide or carbon-based film) that minimizes friction and wear. This layer adapts to temperature-induced changes in the substrate, ensuring consistent performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated CoCrFeNi HEA, the coated material should exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction (targeting values possibly below 0.1–0.2) and an order of magnitude lower wear rate, with these improvements maintained across sliding tests performed from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The typical CoCrFeNi HEA matrix, which under sliding conditions shows an increase in friction coefficient and wear rate at elevated temperatures due to changes in its surface oxidation and deformation behavior.
generation.boundary: Temperature: room temperature to 800 °C; load: representative of typical sliding or tribological testing conditions; environment: ambient air. The effect is anticipated to depend on optimum coating thickness and nanoflake quality.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in friction and wear is uncertain and may depend on precise coating deposition parameters, nanoflake composition, and thickness. Additionally, long-term stability of the tribofilm under cyclic temperature and load variations requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of CoCrFeNi HEA substrates with the applied 2D HEA nanoflake coating (using a controlled deposition method) and an uncoated control group. Subject both groups to identical sliding wear tests under a range of normal loads across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C in ambient air.
measurements: Continuous measurement of the coefficient of friction during sliding
Post-test wear track analysis (via profilometry and SEM) to assess wear rates
Microscopic and compositional analysis (via TEM/EDS) of the worn surfaces to evaluate the formation and stability of the tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire temperature range, or if the adaptive tribofilm is not observed via microstructural analysis, the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Self‐Lubricating Tribo‐Catalytic Activity of 2D High Entropy Alloy Nanoflakes

Abstract: AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have garnered attention due to their remarkable tribological attributes. Predominantly, failure mechanisms in HEAs emanate from stress‐induced dislocations, culminating in crack propagation and film delamination. In this study, we report on the synthesis of 2D HEA of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 which facilitates shear‐induced energy dissipation at sliding interfaces. The ball‐on‐disk tribological investigations demonstrate unprecedentedly low average coefficients of friction (0.076) and wear rates (10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1) under high contact pressures (0.936 GPa) within ambient conditions. Employing multi‐scale characterizations alongside molecular dynamic simulations, we elucidate that the presence of the HEA triggers tribocatalytic activity under high contact pressures emerging as a pivotal factor in extending lubricant lifespan during tribological tests. The resilient lubriciousness coupled with the facile spray coating methodology of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 in ambient environments paves the way for the development of a new class of solid lubricants based on 2D HEA. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
